Settle
SET-l
v.t. & n.
From Anglo-Saxon setl, a seat, and setlan, to place or seat. Webster 1828: to place in a fixed state; to establish; to fix; and as a noun, a seat or bench — the sense the Authorized Version keeps for the ledge of Ezekiel’s altar.

Biblical Definition

Our Lord’s counsel to disciples facing tribunals is that the decision be made long before the summons: Settle it therefore in your hearts, not to meditate before what ye shall answer (Luke 21:14). The settling is of a resolve, not of a speech; He forbids rehearsal precisely because He promises to give a mouth and wisdom in the hour. Peter ends his epistle with the word as the last of four verbs, and the order is a summary of the Christian life: the God of all grace... after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you (1 Peter 5:10). Note where suffering stands — before the settling, not after it, and as the means rather than the obstacle. The word is also a noun in the older English. Ezekiel measures the altar by its ledges: from the bottom upon the ground even to the lower settle shall be two cubits... and from the lesser settle even to the greater settle shall be four cubits (Ezekiel 43:14). And God is said to settle the ground itself: Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers (Psalm 65:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SETTLE as to place in a fixed or permanent condition; to establish; to confirm; to fix; to quiet or compose; and as a noun, a seat, a bench, a place to sit on.

expand to see more

SETTLE, n. — A seat or bench; something to sit on.

SETTLE, v.t. — To place in a fixed or permanent condition; to make firm or stable; to establish.

To fix or establish; to confirm; as, to settle the succession.

To quiet; to compose; to still; as, to settle the mind after agitation.

To adjust; to determine; to close, as an account or a controversy. Anglo-Saxon setl, a seat.

Key Scripture

Luke 21:14 — "Settle it therefore in your hearts, not to meditate before what ye shall answer:"

1 Peter 5:10 — "But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you."

Ezekiel 43:14 — "And from the bottom upon the ground even to the lower settle shall be two cubits, and the breadth one cubit; and from the lesser settle even to the greater settle shall be four cubits, and the breadth one cubit."

Psalm 65:10 — "Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof."

Modern Corruption

1 Peter 5:10 makes suffering the appointed road to a settled soul, which is the opposite of the assumption that affliction is an interruption to be explained away or escaped.

expand to see more

Peter’s sentence has an order that will not be rearranged: after that ye have suffered a while comes first, and then the four verbs — perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle. Suffering is not the obstacle to the settling; it is the means God uses. Two errors run against this from opposite sides. Prosperity teaching treats affliction as a sign of insufficient faith and therefore as something the believer should be able to cancel; the therapeutic instinct treats it as damage whose only meaning is to be recovered from. Scripture treats it as fatherly discipline that yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to them that are exercised thereby (Hebrews 12:11). The 1689 Confession accordingly speaks of God’s wise and holy providence leaving His children for a season to manifold temptations and the corruptions of their own hearts, to humble them and to raise them to a closer dependence on Him.

Luke 21:14 is worth pressing because our Lord forbids something that looks like prudence. Disciples on trial are told not to meditate before what ye shall answer — not to prepare the speech — while being told to settle the resolve in advance. The distinction is exact and pastorally useful: the Christian is to fix beforehand that he will confess Christ, and to leave the wording to the Spirit in the hour. This is not a warrant against study or preparation generally; the same Lord commands His people to be ready always to give an answer (1 Peter 3:15). It is a promise attached to a specific extremity, and the martyrs of the Reformation and after have repeatedly found it kept.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek tithemi (G5087), to place or fix, in the phrase settle in your hearts; themelioo (G2311), to lay a foundation, to settle; Hebrew azarah (H5835), a ledge or enclosure; nachath (H5181), to settle down.

expand to see more

Greek tithemi (G5087) — to place, to set, to fix; Settle it therefore in your hearts (Luke 21:14).

Greek themelioo (G2311) — to lay a foundation, to ground firmly; the fourth verb of 1 Peter 5:10.

Greek sterizo (G4741) — to make stable, to stablish; the second verb of the same sequence.

Hebrew azarah (H5835) — an enclosure or ledge; the settle of Ezekiel’s altar (Ezekiel 43:14).

Hebrew nachath (H5181) — to descend, to settle down; thou settlest the furrows thereof (Psalm 65:10).

Usage

"Settle it therefore in your hearts (Luke 21:14) — the resolve fixed beforehand, the wording left to the hour."

"After that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you (1 Peter 5:10) — suffering stands before the settling, as its means."

"From the lesser settle even to the greater settle (Ezekiel 43:14) — the older English noun, a ledge of the altar."
